“Who’s Doing the Thinking Here?”: A Pedagogy-
First Approach to Integrating Large Language 
Models in Higher Education 
Jonathan Jackson 
Faculty of Science and Engineering 
Queen Mary University of London 
London, UK 
https://orcid.org/0009-0005-3437-8081 
  
Abstract— Large Language Models (LLMs), a subset of 
Generative 
Artificial 
Intelligence 
(GenAI), 
have 
been 
popularised through the widely publicised launch of tools such 
as ChatGPT. While capable of responding to human input in an 
apparently conversational manner, these models do not possess 
understanding in the same way that humans do and their 
outputs, based on probabilistic algorithms, are susceptible to 
presenting falsehoods as facts (hallucinations). Despite the risks, 
there are potential benefits for embedding LLMs in learning 
experiences if educators can cultivate a safe learning 
environment that supports students’ interactions with LLMs 
while empowering students to develop their higher-order 
thinking skills (HOTS). Educators should be empowered to 
make well-informed decisions about the use of LLMs and help 
students work towards co-creation in collaboration with LLMs 
without compromising academic integrity or their own agency. 
In the context of GenAI, the apposite question has become 
“who’s doing the thinking here?”, particularly with the 
prevalence of LLM outputs which are adept at masquerading as 
intelligent thought. Bloom’s revised taxonomy is proposed as an 
effective lens through which educators can evaluate the use of 
LLMs in subject-specific learning contexts, particularly with a 
focus on developing students’ HOTS. Some practical examples 
of prompts are included for educators to try as part of their own 
experimentation with GenAI. This paper aims to empower 
educators by offering an initial set of “Higher Order 
Prompting” principles to support the decision making of how – 
or indeed if – to use LLMs with students, while contributing to 
the ongoing discourse of how Generative AI is impacting Higher 
Education. 
Keywords—Large Language Models, Generative AI, Artificial 
Intelligence, Higher Education, Blooms Taxonomy 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Large Language Models (LLMs) are a type of Generative

I NTRODUCTION Large Language Models (LLMs) are a type of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) which have entered the public consciousness since ChatGPT was released by OpenAI [1] in late 2022. Following their proliferation and widespread adoption, LLMs such as ChatGPT have been used and mis- used in increasingly inventive ways, and the impact on Higher Education (HE) has been, and continues to be, widely discussed [2], [3], [4], [5]. With the impending ubiquity of LLMs, educators must be empowered to make well-informed decisions about the use of LLMs within an educational context while cultivating a safe learning environment that supports students’ interactions with LLMs [6] in a way that enriches their subject-specific learning experience and stimulates higher order thinking rather than eroding it. This paper aims to contribute to the wider discourse around Generative AI in HE and offer the foundations of a theoretical model which can be used by institutions to engage academic staff with the decision-making process of how – or indeed if – to use LLMs within context-specific learning environments. II. L ARGE L ANGUAGE M ODELS LLMs generate text (a response) based on input text (a prompt) from a user and keep track of context across multiple interactions (the context window). While the results are usually impressive, LLMs can present falsities (hallucinations), biased or toxic text, and ignore user instructions [7]. In human terms, at no point are they thinking, reasoning, or understanding [8] despite any claims to the contrary [9]. Bender et al. [10] describe LLMs as “stochastic parrots” which probabilistically stitch words together based on sequences observed in training data, “without any reference to meaning”. Capabilities of GenAI tools such as LLMs are also expanding in an uneven manner, creating a "jagged technological frontier” [11] which is difficult to navigate.
